intro: In Chrome on Mac, press ⌘⇧A (Command, Shift, A) to open Tab Search, type part of a tab's title or site name, then select the match. You can also click the small down arrow at the top right of the tab strip, or type @tabs in the address bar and press Tab.
tldr: Press ⌘⇧A to open Tab Search, type a few words from the tab title or site name, then select the match.
Or click the small down arrow at the top right of the tab strip, or type @tabs in the address bar and press Tab.
Google's help does not say whether search covers every window. Run a two-window test on your own build.
If ⌘⇧A does nothing, click inside the Chrome window first and check whether another app uses the shortcut.
To reopen a tab you closed, press ⌘⇧T.

blocks.text: Chrome gives you three ways to find an open tab on a Mac. All three lead to the same list of tabs, and you pick the one you want from it. The fastest route is the Tab Search shortcut, ⌘⇧A. This guide covers the steps, the parts Google's documentation leaves open, and what to do when the shortcut does nothing.
Search open tabs with the ⌘⇧A shortcut

Tab Search is the feature to use. Google's Chrome Help page for managing tabs names it and lists the Mac shortcut as Command + Shift + A. Press that combination and Chrome opens a search box with your tabs in a list. Google says to enter keywords, then select a tab from the list to open it. That is the whole flow, and it takes a few seconds once you have done it twice.

Keep the search short at first. Add more words only when the list is still long. Start with the site name if you remember it, since a bank or news outlet name narrows the list fast. If the site name matches several tabs, add a distinct word from the page title.
Search tabs with @tabs in the address bar

The address bar gives you the same search. Press ⌘L to move the cursor there, type @tabs, then press Tab or Space. You can also select Search tabs in the suggestions that appear. Enter your keywords and select the tab from the list. Use this route if you already type in the address bar and want to keep your hands in one place.
Use the Tab Search button in the tab strip

The button is the fallback for when the keyboard route fails. Google's help says Tab Search is on by default and pinned in the tab strip. Look at the top right of the tab strip for the small down arrow. Clicking it opens the same tab search box. Use the button when you cannot tell whether the shortcut reached Chrome.

blocks.text: Which windows does Chrome tab search cover on Mac?

This is the part people get wrong, and the official documentation does not settle it. Google's help page does not say whether Tab Search or @tabs covers every window or only the current one. Two third-party guides disagree. Superchargebrowser says the shortcut searches the current window only, and ties its description to Chrome 149. Better Window Switcher says Tab Search covers every Chrome window in the current profile, and it checked this on Chrome 153 and macOS Tahoe 26.

Wikipedia lists 157.0.8103.39 as the current stable build for Windows and macOS, dated 3 November 2026. Guides written for older builds may not match yours, so check your own version. Then run the test below on your Mac.

blocks.title: Test the scope on your Mac
blocks.text: Open a page in the first Chrome window and note a distinct word in its title. Switch to a second Chrome window, press ⌘⇧A, and search for that word. If the tab appears, Tab Search covers both windows.
Find recently closed tabs in Chrome

Tab Search may list recently closed tabs, but only one third-party guide says so. Google's help does not mention closed tabs in the list, so do not count on it. The documented route is ⌘⇧T. Google's help says this reopens previously closed tabs in the order they were closed, so each press steps back one more tab. Use it when you know a tab was open a few minutes ago.
Put Tab Search back in the tab strip

Tab Search is pinned by default, according to Google's help. If you removed it, right-click the button and choose Unpin. Google's page documents that option. To restore the button, open Settings, choose Appearance, and turn on Show tab search button. Google's help gives that path as Settings > Appearance. The page does not name the Mac menu that opens Settings, so look in the Chrome menu in the menu bar.
Other keyboard moves between open tabs

When you know roughly where a tab sits, the keyboard moves you there faster than a search. Google's Chrome keyboard shortcuts page for Mac lists ⌘⌥→ and ⌘⌥← to move to the next and previous tab. Press ⌘1 through ⌘8 to jump to that numbered tab, and ⌘9 to go to the last tab. Use ⌘L to jump to the address bar. These moves do not search. They work by position, so they suit a short, steady tab strip.
Group tabs to shorten the list

Groups keep a long tab strip readable, which makes the search list easier to scan too. Google's help says to right-click a tab, choose Add tab to group, then pick New group or an existing group. To close a whole group, right-click it and select Close group. To reopen a closed group, select More, then Tab groups. Grouping does not replace search, but it shrinks what you have to sort through.
How many open tabs people keep

If your tab count looks wild, you are not alone. PCWorld reports on a 2023 Aalto University study. It says people typically keep 5 to 10 open tabs and 1 to 3 open windows. The range ran from under three tabs to about 400. The study combined an interview study of 16 people with an online survey of 400 people, according to the Aalto research portal.

Closing tabs is one fix, and search is the other. Search lets you find the one you need without first deciding which tabs to keep. About 57% of respondents call browser clutter a mild issue, and almost 25% call it a somewhat or serious concern, according to PCWorld. That split is why search is worth learning even if you never clean up your tabs.
Mistakes people make when searching tabs

items: Pressing ⌘⇧A while another app is in front. Click inside the Chrome window first, so Chrome receives the keystroke.
Assuming the search covers every window. Run the two-window test before you rely on it.
Typing a full web address into the search box. Tab Search works on keywords, so a few words from the title or site name are enough.
Clicking the title when you meant to close the tab. The Close button sits on the right side of each entry in the list.

blocks.text: What this guide does not confirm

A few points stay open. Google's help page is not stamped with a Chrome version, so some version details come from third-party sites. The Mac menu path to Settings is not confirmed on an official page. One unconfirmed claim says right-clicking the Tab Search button opens it, but Google's help documents only the Unpin option, so this guide does not rely on that claim. If you see a difference on your build, trust what you see.
Related Chrome steps on Mac

If you keep the same site open all day, [add it to the Dock in Chrome on Mac](/how-to/add-a-website-to-the-dock-in-chrome) so one click opens it. If you want a private window next to your normal one, [open an incognito window in Chrome on Mac](/how-to/open-an-incognito-window-in-chrome). Both steps cut down on tab hunting.

faq.question: What is the keyboard shortcut to search open tabs in Chrome on Mac?
faq.answer: Press ⌘⇧A, which is Command, Shift and A. Chrome opens Tab Search. Type part of a tab's title or the site name, then select the match. Google's Chrome Help page documents this shortcut for Mac.

faq.question: Why does ⌘⇧A do nothing for me?
faq.answer: Click inside the Chrome window first, since the keystroke may go to the app you used last. If it still fails, leave full screen. Then close background apps one at a time to see whether one of them claims the same shortcut.

faq.question: Does Chrome search tabs in every window on Mac?
faq.answer: Google's help does not say. Superchargebrowser says the search covers the current window only. Better Window Switcher says it covers every window in the current profile. Run the two-window test on your own build to settle it.

faq.question: Can I find a tab I closed by searching?
faq.answer: Only one third-party guide says Tab Search lists recently closed tabs, and Google's help does not confirm it. To reopen a closed tab reliably, press ⌘⇧T, which reopens tabs in the order they were closed.

faq.question: How do I get the Tab Search button back?
faq.answer: Open Settings from the Chrome menu, choose Appearance, and turn on Show tab search button. Google's help documents this path. To hide the button again, right-click it and choose Unpin.

faq.question: How do I search tabs from the address bar?
faq.answer: Click the address bar or press ⌘L, type @tabs, then press Tab or Space. Enter your keywords and select the tab from the list. Google's help describes the same steps.

faq.question: Which Chrome version do these steps cover?
faq.answer: Google's help page is not stamped with a version. Wikipedia lists 157.0.8103.39 as the current stable build for Windows and macOS, dated 3 November 2026. Check your own build from the Chrome menu and run the test if your version differs.

task: Find an open tab in Chrome on Mac
appliesTo: Google Chrome for macOS, desktop app, current stable release
requirements: Google Chrome installed on your Mac
Chrome in front and not in full screen if the shortcut fails
A few open tabs in one or two windows for the test

steps.name: Make Chrome the active app
steps.text: Click an empty spot in the Chrome window, or press ⌘Tab until Chrome is highlighted. The shortcut goes to whichever app has focus, so Chrome must be in front first.
steps.tip: Clicking the page itself is enough. You do not need to select any text first.

steps.name: Press ⌘⇧A to open Tab Search
steps.text: Hold Command and Shift, then press A. Chrome opens Tab Search, a search box with a list of your open tabs. Google's Chrome Help page documents this shortcut for Mac.
steps.tip: The shortcut uses the letter A on the keyboard. If nothing opens, check your keyboard layout.

steps.name: Type part of a tab title or site name
steps.text: Type a word from the page title or the site name, such as a news outlet or a product name. The list narrows as you type. Google says to enter keywords, then select a tab from the list.
steps.tip: Start with the site name. Add a word from the title only if the list is still long.

steps.name: Select the tab you want
steps.text: Move through the matches with the arrow keys, then press Return. You can also click the entry. Google's help says selecting an entry opens that tab.
steps.tip: Each entry has a Close button on its right side. Click it only when you want that tab gone.

steps.name: Search from the address bar with @tabs
steps.text: Press ⌘L to move to the address bar. Type @tabs, then press Tab or Space. Enter your keywords and select the tab from the list. Google documents the same flow on the same help page.
steps.tip: You can also select Search tabs in the suggestions instead of pressing Tab or Space.

steps.name: Use the Tab Search button as a fallback
steps.text: Look at the top right of the tab strip for a small down arrow. Click it to open the same tab search box. Use this when you cannot tell whether the shortcut reached Chrome.
steps.tip: Google's help says Tab Search is pinned in the tab strip by default, so the button should already be there.

steps.name: Test the window scope on your build
steps.text: Open two Chrome windows. In the first, open a page with a distinct word in its title. From the second window, press ⌘⇧A and search for that word. If the tab appears, Tab Search covers both windows.
steps.tip: Pick a title word that no other tab uses, so the test gives a clear answer.

steps.name: Reopen a tab you closed
steps.text: Press ⌘⇧T. Google's help says this reopens previously closed tabs in the order they were closed. Press it again to step back to the tab before that one.
steps.tip: Google does not confirm that closed tabs appear in the search list, so use this shortcut instead.

steps.name: Restore the Tab Search button
steps.text: Open Settings from the Chrome menu, then choose Appearance. Turn on Show tab search button. The button returns to the tab strip.
steps.tip: To remove it again, right-click the button and select Unpin.

troubleshooting.fix: Click inside the Chrome window first, because the keystroke may go to the app you used last. If it still fails, leave full screen. A third-party guide says full screen can block the shortcut.

troubleshooting.problem: Another app seems to take the shortcut
troubleshooting.fix: A third-party guide says another running app, or an OS-level binding, can claim ⌘⇧A before Chrome gets it. Quit background apps one at a time and test after each to find the conflict.

troubleshooting.problem: The Tab Search button is missing
troubleshooting.fix: Open Settings, choose Appearance, and turn on Show tab search button. Google's help gives this as the way to bring it back.

troubleshooting.problem: The tab I want is not in the list
troubleshooting.fix: Try fewer keywords, then try the site name instead of the title. If it still does not appear, the tab may sit in a window outside the search scope. Run the two-window test to check.

troubleshooting.problem: @tabs in the address bar does nothing
troubleshooting.fix: Type @tabs exactly, then press Tab or Space. You can also select Search tabs from the suggestions, as Google's help describes.
